The fluorescence observed is caused by the precipitation of magnesium pyrophosphate or the use of a non-inhibitory fluorescing reagent that becomes quenched in the presence of divalent cations. Figure 1 illustrates calcein, which remains unquenched due to the consumption of divalent cations by pyrophosphate, fluorescing under ultraviolet (UV) light. The resulting turbid and fluorescent product is easily visible to the naked eye. 2. The test procedure for TB-LAMP involves three main steps, as shown in Figure 2: Sample Preparation: Bacteria are heat-treated to achieve inactivation and lysis, which also facilitates DNA extraction. Amplification: The sample is incubated in a heating block at 67°C, where the polymerase enzyme amplifies the target DNA. Visualization: The reaction tube contains a double-stranded DNA-binding molecule that fluoresces under UV light, allowing for easy detection with the naked eye. 3. The TB-LAMP workflow includes the following steps: Transfer and lyse the sputum sample. Extract DNA using the Loopamp™ PURE DNA extraction method. Perform loop-mediated isothermal amplification. Read the results visually under UV light. 4. To process sputum samples, use a pipette to collect the most purulent portion of each sample. Slowly transfer 60 µL of sputum into a heating tube and incubate it at 90°C for 5 minutes in the HumaLoop T heating unit. Extract 30 µL of DNA directly into the reaction tube by squeezing the adsorbent tube. Incubate the reaction tube at 67°C for 40 minutes in the reaction unit. Positive results fluoresce green under UV light. 5. The TB-LAMP assay is a loop-mediated isothermal amplification test designed for the detection of tuberculosis (TB). It is particularly useful in settings with intermediate or high TB burdens. However, it does not replace the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, which simultaneously detects TB and rifampicin resistance and is automated. 6. The diagnostic accuracy of TB-LAMP was evaluated in various scenarios: As a replacement for sputum-smear microscopy. As an add-on test for individuals with negative sputum-smear microscopy results. In comparison with the Xpert MTB/RIF assay for detecting pulmonary TB. 7. The systematic review identified 20 studies evaluating TB-LAMP on sputum samples from adults with suspected pulmonary TB in settings with intermediate or high TB burdens. Studies used mycobacterial culture as the reference standard, with three hierarchical culture-based standards to assess diagnostic accuracy. 8. The cost-effectiveness analysis compared TB-LAMP and Xpert MTB/RIF as routine diagnostic tests in peripheral laboratories in Malawi and Vietnam. TB-LAMP was found to be a cost-effective alternative in settings where Xpert MTB/RIF could not be implemented due to infrastructure limitations, such as the lack of a continuous power supply. 9. TB-LAMP has limitations, including its inability to detect rifampicin-resistant TB and suboptimal sensitivity in people living with HIV (PLHIV). National policymakers must carefully evaluate operational feasibility and cost considerations before adopting this technology. 10. The lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assay detects the LAM antigen in urine and is a potential point-of-care test for TB. While its sensitivity is suboptimal for general TB diagnosis, it shows improved sensitivity in individuals co-infected with HIV, particularly those with low CD4 cell counts. 11. The Alere Determine TB LAM Ag (Alere LAM) is the only commercially available urinary LAM test. It is recommended as a rule-in test for TB in patients with advanced HIV-induced immunosuppression to facilitate early initiation of anti-TB treatment. 12. Recommendations for LF-LAM use include: In inpatient settings, it is strongly recommended for individuals with advanced HIV disease or who are seriously ill, regardless of TB symptoms. In outpatient settings, it is conditionally recommended for individuals with CD4 cell counts below 100 cells/mm³, irrespective of TB symptoms. 13. LF-LAM should be used as an add-on to clinical judgment and in combination with other diagnostic methods. It does not replace the need for sputum-based tests like Xpert MTB/RIF, which remains the preferred initial diagnostic test for pulmonary TB.
